title: JANUARY 2026
overview: Journalism and Technology Trends and Predictions 2026 by Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism Nic Newman’s report examines the pressures facing journalism and publishers in 2026, including AI-driven changes to search and content, competition from creators, platform shifts, misinformation, newsroom AI adoption, and business-model challenges. It draws on a survey of senior digital leaders and combines survey results with analysis and predictions for the year ahead. Covers journalism and technology trends, challenges, and predictions for 2026, including AI, audience traffic, content and distribution strategies, misinformation, newsroom practices, and business models. Draws on an industry survey of digital leaders from 51 countries and territories; the excerpts do not identify specific geographic regions.
methods: Industry survey of a strategic sample of 280 digital leaders from 51 countries and territories; question-specific bases include 273 respondents (Q9) and 264 (Q13).

Chartbeat analytics data on page-view referrals aggregated across more than 2,000 news websites and apps in its network; the report also describes aggregate Google Search traffic to hundreds of news sites.
Background conversations, interviews, and emails with publishers, academics, and industry experts provided additional input.
key_findings: Publishers’ average expectation was that search-engine traffic would fall 43% over the next three years.
From November 2024 to November 2025, Google Search referrals in the global Chartbeat network fell 33% year on year.
For possible news-content licensing deals with AI companies in about three years, 20% of publisher respondents expected a significant source of income.
For possible news-content licensing deals with AI companies in about three years, 49% of publisher respondents expected a minor contribution.
For possible news-content licensing deals with AI companies in about three years, 20% of publisher respondents expected no income.
The net difference between respondents planning more versus less focus was +91 for original investigations and on-the-ground reporting.
limitations: Publisher expectations that misinformation and AI-generated content could strengthen news media may be wishful thinking; audience uncertainty about truth does not necessarily mean they will return to news media.
Fewer than 1% of news images or videos published globally include C2PA metadata; adoption requires ecosystem-wide buy-in, and metadata can be stripped at any stage.
Content-detection systems have so far been only partly effective; some experts suggest TikTok automatically detects less than half of AI-generated content.

sections.summary: Introduces Nic Newman and his work in digital media and journalism. It notes his role at the Reuters Institute and his experience in BBC digital journalism and media strategy.
key_points: Newman is a Senior Research Associate at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism.
He was a founding member of the BBC News Website and later led product development for BBC Journalism sites.

The author credits Institute colleagues and other publishers, academics, and industry experts for their input.
